```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
shot <- function(file, width = "100%") knitr::include_graphics(file.path("images", file))
```

This tutorial walks through one complete run of `stimulus_pipeline.praat` on the demo
recording that comes with the script. It takes about five minutes. The screenshots are from runs
on the two demo recordings, so you can follow along and should see the same windows.

The demo recording (`example/demo_list.wav`) is synthetic speech: eight English words, each said
three times in a row. One mistake is built in. After the first *river*, the speaker says "um". The
script will find 25 words where the list expects 24, and you will fix that by hand.

You need Praat (tested with version 6.4.43).

Later sections cover how to choose settings for your own stimuli, and how to let the script tune
the segmentation settings on a stretch of your recording that you have corrected by hand.

# Prepare the input

The script needs two things: a recording and a CSV with the words in the order they were read.

```{r show-csv}
words <- read.csv("../example/demo_list.csv")
words
```

Each word is listed **once**, even though it was said three times. You tell the script about the
repetitions in the form. The column name (`stimuli`) is the script's default. If your column has
another name, you type it into the form. Extra columns are fine and are ignored.

If you keep your word list in R, writing the CSV is one line:

```{r write-csv, eval = FALSE}
write.csv(data.frame(stimuli = c("apple", "banana", "window")),
          "my_list.csv", row.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
```

A few things make the automatic segmentation work well:

- leave a clear pause (about half a second or more) between tokens,
- start the recording with a second or so of silence,
- if a speaker stumbles, have them repeat the word rather than restart the list. The extra token is
  then easy to spot and label as `xxx`, as you will do below.

# Open and run the script

In Praat, choose **Praat > Open Praat script...** and open `stimulus_pipeline.praat`.
The script window opens. The comment block at the top summarises what the script does.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "The script window. Run it with Run > Run, or Ctrl+R."}
shot("01_script_editor.png")
```

Choose **Run > Run** (or press Ctrl+R). The form appears.

# Fill in the form

This is the form with its default values. The sound file and csv file already point to the demo:

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "70%", fig.cap = "The form with its default values."}
shot("02_form_defaults.png")
```

For the demo, change three fields:

| Field | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| repetitions per word | `3` | each word was said three times in a row, so the script expects 8 x 3 = 24 words |
| output folder | `example/output` | results go into `example/output/demo_list/` |
| export repetitions | `2` | also collect every second repetition into its own folder (for example, if you want the middle token of each word) |

Relative paths are read relative to the folder the script is in, so these work as long as the
`example` folder sits next to the script, wherever you put the two. For your own recordings, type
the path to your files the same way, relative to the script (`recordings/speaker01.wav`) or in
full.

You can use `/` or `\` in paths on any computer. The script turns every `\` into `/` before it
opens a file, and Praat reads `/` on Windows, Mac and Linux alike. So a path typed on a Windows
machine (`example\demo_list.wav`) still works when the same settings are used on a Mac. Forward
slashes are the safest habit.

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "70%", fig.cap = "The form filled in for the demo."}
shot("03_form_filled.png")
```

Leave the cutting and normalization settings at their defaults for now: 20 ms of padding from the
recording around each word, 5 ms fades, no normalization. The [README on GitHub](https://github.com/maypychan/praat-stimulus-pipeline#readme) describes every field.

For this tutorial, also tick **advanced settings**, so you can see what is there. Then click **OK**.

## Advanced settings (optional)

Because *advanced settings* was ticked, a second window opens before anything happens.

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "70%", fig.cap = "The advanced settings. The defaults work for most recordings."}
shot("04_advanced.png")
```

The first block is the silence detection itself. The silence threshold is in dB below the loudest
point of the recording, so -30 means "anything 30 dB quieter than the peak counts as silence".
The next two blocks repair the two most common segmentation errors:

- **Merge split words** joins two pieces across a short pause (under 0.35 s) when the joined word
  is not much longer than a typical word. This repairs words split at a stop closure, such as the
  silent gap in *back-pack*.
- **Widen edges** extends each word outward while the sound stays above -40 dB, so that weak
  onsets and offsets (the /f/ of *feather*, a final /s/) are not cut off.

The *checks* block sets which words get flagged as suspiciously short or long. Click **Continue**.
Most of the time you can leave *advanced settings* unticked and skip this window.

# Fix the word count

The script segments the recording and counts the words. The demo has 25 sounding intervals (24
words and the "um"), but the CSV expects 24. So the TextGrid editor opens, with a pause window
explaining the problem.

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "70%", fig.cap = "The script found one word too many."}
shot("06_fix_pause.png")
```

The editor shows the recording with two tiers:

- **Tier 1 (`silences`)** is the segmentation. Pauses are labelled `xxx`; words are empty. This is
  the tier you edit, and the only one used for cutting.
- **Tier 2 (`guide`)** numbers the words and shows which CSV word each will receive, along with any
  warnings. It is rebuilt every time you click *Recheck*, so there is no point editing it.

Zoomed in around 15 s, the problem is visible:

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Word 10 is river, but word 11 is the short 'um'. Because of it, the guide expects river at 11 and backpack at 13, one word too early."}
shot("05_fix_editor.png")
```

To zoom in, drag across the waveform to select a stretch and press Ctrl+N (or click **sel** at the
bottom left). Click **all** to see the whole recording again. You can play a selection with the
Tab key, which is the quickest way to find out what an interval contains.

The guide tier is the key to finding the error. Read along it: *10 river*, *11 river*, *12 river*,
*13 backpack*. But the waveform shows three tokens of *river* and one short token between the first
two. Wherever the guide labels stop matching what you hear, the mistake is at or just before that
point.

## Make the fix

The "um" is not a list word, so label it as a pause. Click inside its interval on tier 1 to select
it, and type `xxx`.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "The 'um' interval on tier 1 now reads xxx. The guide tier will update after Recheck."}
shot("07_fix_typed.png")
```

The other common fixes work the same way, all on tier 1:

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| a cough, breath, click or false start was taken as a word | label it `xxx` |
| one word was split into two intervals | remove the boundaries around the `xxx` gap between the pieces (click a boundary and press Alt+Backspace), then delete the leftover `xxx` text so the joined interval is empty |
| two words were merged into one interval | click in the pause between them and press Enter to add a boundary. Add a second one and label the stretch between them `xxx`, so the pause stays silent |
| a word was missed entirely | add boundaries at its start and end, and leave the interval empty |

Leave the word intervals themselves empty. If you type text into one, the script reports it as
*stray text* and offers a **Stray text = silence** button that turns such labels into `xxx`.

Click **Recheck** in the pause window. If the count still does not match, the editor comes back
with an updated guide tier. Repeat until it matches. Do not close the editor window yourself;
always use the buttons in the pause window.

# Check the labels

Once the count is right, the script writes the CSV words into tier 1 and opens the editor again
for a final check.

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "70%", fig.cap = "The final check: all 24 words are labelled, with no warnings."}
shot("08_check_pause.png")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "The same stretch as before. The three rivers are labelled river, and the 'um' stays xxx."}
shot("09_check_editor.png")
```

This is the moment to check the boundaries, since they decide where each file is cut. Listen to a
few words and look for clipped onsets or offsets. If you move a boundary, the labels stay as they
are. If you add or remove boundaries, click **Relabel from csv** to fill in the words again in
order. Relabelling replaces anything you typed by hand. If the count no longer matches, the script
goes back to the fixing step.

The summary in the pause window lists any warnings. A clean run says "No problems flagged". The
warnings are:

- **SHORT**: a word under 100 ms, often a click or half of a split word,
- **LONG**: a word over 1.5 s, often two words merged,
- **SHIFT**: the pause pattern suggests the labels are off by one or two words in some stretch. When
  each word is repeated, pauses between different words tend to be longer than pauses between
  repetitions, and the script checks whether the labels line up with that pattern. This needs at
  least 30 words, so it does not run on the 24-word demo.

All flags also appear on the guide tier, and the Info window lists them with times.

When you are happy, click **Cut stimuli**.

# The output

The script cuts, processes and saves every word, and reports each file in the Info window.

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "80%", fig.cap = "The Info window after cutting: one line per file, then a summary."}
shot("10_info.png")
```

The output folder `example/output/demo_list/` now contains:

```
demo_list/
├── apple_1.wav  apple_2.wav  apple_3.wav
├── banana_1.wav banana_2.wav banana_3.wav
├── ...                                     (24 WAV files)
├── demo_list.TextGrid                      the final labelled TextGrid
├── demo_list_log.csv                       one row per file
├── sf_dur_2.csv                            durations of the stims_2 files
└── stims_2/
    ├── apple_2.wav
    ├── banana_2.wav
    └── ...                                 (8 WAV files, one per word)
```

Repeated words are numbered in recording order, so `river_2.wav` is the second *river* the speaker
said, not counting the "um". A word that occurs only once in the recording gets no number.

If you run the script again on the same recording, it asks whether to overwrite the folder or save
into a new one (`demo_list_2`, `demo_list_3`, ...). Overwriting replaces files with the same names
and leaves any others in place.

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "70%", fig.cap = "Running the script a second time on the same recording."}
shot("16_folder_in_use.png")
```

## The log file

The log records where every file came from. A copy from the demo run is in
`example/demo_output/`:

```{r log}
log <- read.csv("../example/demo_output/demo_list_log.csv")
knitr::kable(head(log, 9), digits = 3)
```

`start` and `end` are the word's position in the original recording, in seconds. `word_ms` is the
word itself and `file_ms` the whole file, here 40 ms longer because of the 20 ms of padding on each
side. `clipped` is 1 if the file's peak went above 1, which happens most often with RMS
normalization to a high target.

Because the log keeps the original times, you can always go back from a stimulus file to the
moment in the recording it came from.

## Checking the stimuli in R

The log is also a quick way to look for outliers before you use the stimuli. For example,
the duration of every token, by word:

```{r durations, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 7, fig.cap = "Word durations in the demo, three tokens per word. The grey bar marks each word's mean."}
library(ggplot2)

log$label <- factor(log$label, levels = unique(log$label))
ggplot(log, aes(x = label, y = word_ms)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.5, linewidth = 0.3,
               colour = "grey55") +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 1),
             size = 2.5, colour = "#1f4e8c") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Word duration (ms)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

A token far from the others of the same word usually points to a boundary worth checking in the
TextGrid. With real speakers, expect much more spread than in this synthetic demo.

`sf_dur_2.csv` lists the files that were copied into `stims_2/`, with their durations in seconds:

```{r sfdur}
knitr::kable(read.csv("../example/demo_output/sf_dur_2.csv"), digits = 3)
```

# Choosing settings for your stimuli

The defaults were chosen for a careful reader in a quiet room, saying words of one to three
syllables with clear pauses. If your recording is like that, leave them alone. If it is not, you
can usually work out better settings from three things you already know: **what the words sound
like**, **how the speaker paced the list**, and **how noisy the recording is**.

## Measure first

Two numbers are worth checking before changing anything.

- **The noise floor.** The Info window reports it at the start of every run, in dB below the
  loudest point of the recording (`Noise floor (10th percentile of the intensity): -54.0 dB re.
  maximum` for the quiet demo above, and -34.2 dB for the noisy demo in the next section). The
  silence threshold must sit clearly above it. The script warns you when it is less than 10 dB
  above.
- **The pauses.** Open the recording in Praat (**View & Edit**), select a few typical pauses
  between tokens and read their duration at the top of the selection. Do the same for the longest
  silent gap *inside* a word, such as the closure in *backpack* or a geminate. Every
  segmentation setting is about telling these two kinds of silence apart.

## The segmentation settings

All of these are in the **advanced settings** window.

| Setting | What it decides | Choose it from |
|---|---|---|
| Silence threshold (-30 dB) | how quiet a frame must be to count as silence, relative to the loudest point | the noise floor: at least 10 dB above it. Lower (e.g. -35) keeps weak sounds such as /f/, /h/ and breathy offsets inside the word; higher (e.g. -25) copes with background noise |
| Minimum silent interval (0.2 s) | the shortest pause that separates two words | must be **longer** than the longest silence inside a word, and **shorter** than the shortest pause between tokens |
| Minimum sounding interval (0.1 s) | the shortest sound that counts as a word | shorter than your shortest word (very short words such as *egg* or *up* can be around 0.15 s), longer than clicks and lip smacks |
| Merge split words: max pause (0.35 s) | pauses shorter than this may be joined across | shorter than the pauses *between* tokens, or repetitions said close together get joined |
| Merge split words: max ratio (1.6) | a join is only made if the result is at most this many times the median word | raise it (to 2-2.5) when your list mixes short and long words, so a split long word can still be rejoined |
| Widen edges: edge threshold (-40 dB), edge max (0.2 s) | how far each word is extended outward into quieter sound | lower the threshold (-45) for weak fricative onsets and offsets; turn widening off if you want the tightest possible cuts |
| Minimum pitch (100 Hz) | the window of the intensity analysis | 75 Hz for low or creaky voices; a lower value smooths the intensity more, so very short pauses can disappear |
| Short / long interval (100 / 1500 ms) | which words get the `SHORT` and `LONG` flags | just below your shortest and just above your longest expected word |
| Check repetition pattern | the `SHIFT` flags | turn it off if the speaker did not pause longer between different words than between repetitions |

The threshold is relative to the loudest moment in the whole file. A single loud cough, laugh or
microphone bump at the start raises that reference, so ordinary speech then looks quiet and words
start to split. If that happens, trim the bump before running the script, or raise the threshold.
The **auto threshold** option sets the threshold from the recording's own intensity distribution
(halfway between its 25th and 75th percentiles), which can help when you do not know where to start.

## The cutting settings

These are in the main form, and they depend on what the stimuli are for rather than on the
recording.

- **Padding** keeps real audio from the recording around each word. Keep at least 20 ms so release
  bursts, final aspiration and fricative tails are not cut. Use more (30-50 ms) for words ending in
  voiceless stops or fricatives, but no more than about half the shortest pause, or the padding
  will pick up the neighbouring word.
- **Fade** removes clicks at the file edges. Keep it **shorter than the padding** (5 ms with 20 ms of
  padding), so the fade falls on the padding and not on the word itself.
- **Amplitude normalization.** `intensity (RMS)` gives every word roughly the same loudness, which
  is what most perception experiments need. It is measured on the word without the padding. `peak`
  gives every file the same maximum, which is safer against clipping but leaves loudness
  differences. With RMS, check the `clipped` column of the log; if any file clipped, lower *target
  intensity db* (e.g. to 65).
- **Target duration** stretches or compresses every word with Praat's overlap-add method. It sounds
  natural for moderate changes (up to about 1.5 times) on voiced speech, less so for large ones.

## Examples

| Your recording | What to change |
|---|---|
| A quiet booth, one- to three-syllable words, clear pauses | nothing |
| Words with long closures inside them (*bookcase*, *hotdog*, geminates in Italian or Japanese, tense stops in Korean), and some of them come out split | keep *merge split words* on. If they are still split and the pauses between tokens are longer than 0.4 s, raise *minimum silent interval* to 0.25-0.3 s |
| A list that mixes one-syllable and five-syllable words | *merge max ratio* 2-2.5, *long interval* 2000-2500 ms |
| A laptop or phone microphone, a fan or traffic in the background | check the noise floor and raise the threshold to at least 10 dB above it (-25 or -20 dB), or use *tune settings* |
| A fast reader, about 0.25 s between repetitions | *minimum silent interval* 0.15 s and *merge max pause* 0.2 s, so repetitions are neither merged by silence detection nor joined afterwards |
| Many weak onsets (*feather*, *thimble*, *honey*, vowel-initial words) | *silence threshold* -35 dB and *edge threshold* -45 dB, as long as the noise floor allows it |
| A low, creaky voice | *minimum pitch* 75 Hz |

When you are unsure between two settings, you do not have to guess: correct a stretch of the
recording by hand and let the script compare them, as the next section shows.

# Tuning the settings on your recording

For long recordings it pays to spend a few minutes correcting the start by hand and letting the
script find the settings that best reproduce your corrections. This section does that on the
second demo, `example/demo_tuning.wav`: twelve words said three times each, with background noise
loud enough that the default settings merge words.

## Start a tuning run

Set the form as below and tick **tune settings**:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| sound file | `example/demo_tuning.wav` |
| csv file | `example/demo_tuning.csv` |
| repetitions per word | `3` |
| output folder | `example/output` |
| tune settings | ticked |
| tuning stretch s | `20` |

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "70%", fig.cap = "The form for a tuning run."}
shot("11_form_tuning.png")
```

*tuning stretch s* sets how much of the start you will correct. The demo is only 42 s long, so
20 s is plenty. For a real recording, keep the default 180 s or pick a stretch that holds at
least 50-100 tokens and the kinds of problems you expect in the rest. The stretch must contain at
least 10 words.

## Correct the stretch

The script segments the recording with the current settings, marks the stretch on a `tuning`
tier, and pauses.

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "70%", fig.cap = "The tuning pause window. The stretch here runs from 0 to 22 s, ending in the middle of a pause."}
shot("12_tune_pause.png")
```

Correct tier 1 inside the stretch so that it is right: every list word in its own empty interval,
everything else (pauses, coughs, false starts, extra words) labelled `xxx`, with the boundaries at
the word edges. You can move the end of the stretch by dragging the boundary on the `tuning` tier.

In the demo, the noise fills some pauses, so pairs of words come out as one interval. Here the
third *hotdog* and the first *island* were merged:

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Before correcting: the long interval in the middle holds two words."}
shot("13_tune_editor.png")
```

To split them, click at the end of *hotdog* on tier 1 and press Enter to add a boundary, do the
same at the start of *island*, and label the new interval between them `xxx`:

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "After correcting: one word per interval, and the pause between them labelled xxx."}
shot("14_tune_corrected.png")
```

Do this for every error in the stretch. The scoring trusts your corrections, so take care with
them; a mistake left in the stretch counts against the settings that got that word right. Then
click **Test settings**. (**Skip tuning** goes straight on to the normal run with the current
settings.)

## Read the result

The script scores 150 combinations of four settings on your stretch, plus the current settings:

- silence threshold: -20, -25, -30, -35, -40 dB
- minimum silent interval: 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.35 s
- minimum sounding interval: 0.05, 0.1, 0.15 s
- merge split words: on or off

For each one it counts the corrections you would have had to make: words split in two, words
merged together, words missed, and short extra intervals. It switches to the best combination only
if that needs at least 3 corrections, and 30%, fewer than the current settings; otherwise it keeps
your settings. The result is at the top of the Info window:

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "The tuning result. The default settings would have needed 6 corrections in the stretch, the best ones none, so the script switched to them."}
shot("15_tune_info.png")
```

In the demo, the defaults (-30 dB) would have needed 6 corrections in the stretch, all merges.
The best settings need none, and the script switched to a threshold of -25 dB. The noise-floor
warning still appears, because -25 dB is less than 10 dB above the floor of -34 dB. The warning is
a rule of thumb; your corrected stretch is direct evidence, and here it shows -25 dB works.

The corrected stretch is kept as you left it, and the new settings are used only from the end of
the stretch onward. In the demo, that was enough for the whole recording: the count matched at the
first check, so the script skipped the fixing step and went straight to the final label check.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "The final check after tuning: the stretch you corrected, now labelled from the CSV."}
shot("17_tune_labelled.png")
```

## The tuning table

Every setting's score is saved in `<recording>_tuning.csv` in the output folder. A copy from the
demo run is in `example/demo_output/`:

```{r tuning-table}
tuning <- read.csv("../example/demo_output/demo_tuning_tuning.csv")
knitr::kable(head(tuning[, 1:11], 6))
```

`to_fix` is the total number of corrections (`splits + merges + missed + short_extra`). Long extra
intervals (`long_extra`, 0.25 s or more) are not counted, because they are usually real extra
productions that you would label `xxx` anyway. Rows with the same `to_fix` are sorted by how close
they are to your current settings, so the script prefers the smallest change that works.
`current = 1` marks the settings you started with:

```{r tuning-current}
knitr::kable(tuning[tuning$current == 1, 1:11])
```

The table also shows how sensitive the recording is to each setting. Here, the threshold is what
matters:

```{r tuning-plot, fig.height = 3.6, fig.width = 7, fig.cap = "Corrections needed in the demo stretch, by silence threshold and minimum silent interval (minimum sounding 0.1 s, merging on). Darker cells need more corrections."}
sub <- subset(tuning, current == 0 & min_sounding == 0.1 & merge == 1)
ggplot(sub, aes(x = factor(threshold), y = factor(min_silent), fill = to_fix)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = to_fix, colour = to_fix > max(to_fix) / 2), size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#eef3fb", high = "#1f4e8c", guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#1b1b1b", `TRUE` = "white"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Silence threshold (dB re. maximum)", y = "Minimum silent interval (s)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

At -20 and -25 dB every minimum silent interval works. From -30 dB down, the noise starts to fill
the pauses and the counts climb quickly. On a quiet recording the grid is usually low across a
wide range of settings, and the script keeps yours.

## Tips for tuning

- Tune once per speaker or recording setup, then note the settings and type them into the
  advanced settings for later recordings made the same way.
- Tuning only tries the four settings above. Merge max pause and ratio, edge widening and minimum
  pitch stay as you set them, so set those first from what you know about the stimuli.
- If the script keeps your settings, it found nothing clearly better, and the tuning table shows
  how close the alternatives came. Your corrections are kept either way, so the time is not lost.

# Going further

**Normalizing the stimuli.** Set *amplitude normalization* to `peak` to scale every file to the
same peak, or to `intensity (RMS)` to give every word the same loudness (*target intensity db*).
Set *target duration ms* above 0 to stretch or compress every word to the same duration. The order
of processing is: cut the word, normalize its duration, add padding, fade, normalize amplitude, add
silence.

**Adding silence.** *leading silence ms* and *trailing silence ms* add digital silence before and
after each file, for example to give every stimulus the same onset delay in an experiment.

**When something goes wrong.** **Stop** in any pause window ends the script but leaves the Sound
and TextGrid in the Praat Objects window. You can save the TextGrid from there (**Save > Save as
text file...**) so your edits are not lost. The [README on GitHub](https://github.com/maypychan/praat-stimulus-pipeline#readme) has a troubleshooting list for common
error messages.
